Protocol “layers” and reference models 

Networks are complex, with many “pieces”:  

- Hosts 
    

- Routers 
    

- Links of various media 
    

- Applications 
    

- Protocols 
    

- Hardware, software 
    

Service model in Layered Internet 

Internet is organized as a stack of layers 

- To reduce design complexity 
    

- Ease of maintenance 
    

Service model: 

- Each layer provides services to the layer above, 
    

- The implementation details are abstracted (hidden), ensuring modularity and independence between layers. 
    

Top to bottom: 

5 – Application Layer 

4 – Transport Layer 

3 – Network Layer 

2 – Link Layer 

1 – Physical Layer 

Client – Server (Apache)  

Web client makes a request for [www.Radford.edu/index.html](https://www.Radford.edu/index.html)  

Application Layer – Client Puts the request into a message header – Apache receives it as an HTTP message 

This is Network Applications Communications 

Transport Layer – TCP Header added before the message header – Apache receives it as a TCP segment, below the HTTP message 

This is Process-to-Process Communication 

Network Layer – Ip Header added before the TCP header – Apache receives it as an IP Datagram 

This is Host-to-Host Communication 

Link Layer – MAC header added before IP Header – Apache receives it as a Frame 

This is Adjacent-Nodes Communication 

Physical layer – literally bits, the entire thing is translated into bits – Apache receives this as bits 

This is bits on the wire 

![](data:image/png;base64,) 

Layered Internet protocol stack 

Application: supporting network applications  

- HTTP, IMAP, SMTP, DNS 
    

Transport: Process-process data transfer 

- TCP, UDP 
    

Network: routing of datagrams from source to destination 

- IP, routing protocols 
    

Link: Data transfer between neighboring network elements 

- Ethernet, 802.11 (Wi-Fi), PPP 
    

Physical 

- Bits on the wire 
    

Services, Layering, and Encapsulation 

All of these layers added into one is called a Frame.
